transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is good to see you again, Ms. Osei. I wanted to start today by being very direct with you about a mistake that occurred with your last immunotherapy dose. We gave the medication on the wrong day of your cycle because of a calendar entry error. Instead of the scheduled date, it was administered early. Does that make sense so far?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I was wondering why the clinic called me in earlier than usual. You are saying the dosing schedule was missed?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, that is exactly what happened. In this specific treatment, the timing between doses is designed to maximize how the drug interacts with your immune system. By giving it too early, we deviated from the clinical protocol. Are you following me on the timing aspect of this?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I follow you. As a nurse practitioner, I'm familiar with cycle intervals. My concern is the efficacy. This isn't a minor administrative slip; this is a deviation from the standard of care.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can hear how unsettling that is. Knowing the clinical standards yourself, it must feel incredibly frustrating to know those standards weren't met in your own care.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It is more than frustrating. It is a breach of professional trust. I trust my team to be precise with these intervals because the efficacy depends on it. How does this actually impact my prognosis?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is a very valid question. While we can't say for certain, administering a dose early can potentially reduce the effectiveness of that specific cycle.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Which is exactly why—

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are currently reviewing the literature on similar timing errors.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I wasn't finished. If the efficacy is compromised, we are talking about a window of time where my cancer might not be suppressed as it should be. That is a significant risk.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I completely recognize that the stakes feel incredibly high right now. It is scary to think that your progress might be stalled because of a scheduling mistake.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It is not just scary, it is an avoidable error. Who was responsible for the calendar entry? Was this a systemic failure in the software or a human error in data entry?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The entries were mismanaged during the scheduling process. The system relies on manual input, and the wrong date was selected.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So someone just typed it in wrong. I'm surprised that a double-check system didn't catch this before the infusion started.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand why you'd expect that level of redundancy. It is disappointing that it didn't happen here.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Disappointing is a very mild word. I expect a formal apology and a clear explanation of how you intend to rectify the dosing for the rest of the cycle.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We have a plan to move forward. I have consulted with the attending oncologist, and we have decided to shift the subsequent doses to get you back on the original rhythm. You will come in on the 14th of next month instead of the 10th. I need you to mark that in your own calendar to ensure we are aligned.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And what about the missed window? Are we just hoping for the best, or is there a compensatory dose?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There is no compensatory dose for immunotherapy, but we will move your next scan up by two weeks to monitor for any change in response. I will call you tomorrow morning to confirm the appointment time for that scan.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I appreciate the scan. But I still feel that the gravity of the error hasn't been fully acknowledged. This was a failure of basic clinical safety.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know it's hard to feel secure in the process after this. It's a heavy realization that your care wasn't precise.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Precisely. As a clinician, I can't help but think about the documentation. Is this being filed as an incident report?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are processing the internal paperwork now. Look, I really have to go to my next appointment in a couple of minutes, so let's wrap this up.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm sorry, you're rushing me now? I am trying to discuss the safety protocols of the clinic that failed me.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I just want to make sure we get you out on time. We've established the shift in the schedule and the early scan.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: We have not established how you will prevent this from happening to the next patient.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are reviewing the scheduling workflow with the nursing staff.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is vague. I want a specific change in protocol.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are looking into a second-person verification for all immunotherapy dates. I'll have to get back to you on when that becomes policy. I really have to get to the other room now.

H.justification: Resident interrupts the patient at [00:01:35] and uses rushing language repeatedly at the end of the encounter.

E.justification: Error named in first turn, used lay language, and checked comprehension twice ('Does that make sense so far?' and 'Are you following me...?').

A.justification: No direct apology language ('I'm sorry' or 'I apologize') was used throughout the transcript.

R.justification: Resident named specific emotions ('unsettling', 'frustrating', 'scary') and referenced the patient's professional background as a clinician.

T.justification: Provided specific next steps (date of 14th, early scan), assigned a patient role (mark calendar), and addressed prevention (second-person verification).
